label: <DEL> step of long sequences whose first token is in {o,g,t,y,k,2,3,e,r,l,q}
explanation: Almost exclusively a delimiter-step unit: 98.8% of activation mass is on the <DEL> step (recall_idx 0), with small traces on the last original tokens of long sequences and essentially nothing in the copy phase. It fires on only ~12% of delimiters, though. Two things gate it, and both act in a graded way. (1) Length: rate on the delimiter rises steeply with L (L=9 about 33%, L=8 about 24%, L<=5 under 1%), and L>=8 carries about 83% of the mass. (2) The first original token, which is the token about to be output: o, g, t, y and k are strongest (lift about 5x), then 2, 3, e, r, l, q. The second original token (next_out) has a similar but weaker effect. Top activations combine L=8-9 with a first token like o/g/t/y. It does not fire on delimiters of short sequences or of sequences that start with other tokens (e.g. i, c, u, z, x, f, d). No boolean predicate gets past F1 of about 0.54, because the response looks additive over length and the first two tokens rather than a hard conjunction. A variant that also accepts the second token in the set gets mass recall of about 0.94 but lower precision.

scorecard.summary: Graded preference over the token being output (most: o, g, t, y, k, e; least: f, i, s, u) and the next token to output (most: k, 2, g, y, t, o; least: u, s, i, f); timing cues that raise it most: phase=1, recall_idx=0, L=9 & t=9.
